quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: At midday, sunlight travels through a thin layer of air and looks white. At sunset, the sun is low, so its light must cross a much thicker layer of atmosphere. Along the way, blue light is scattered in all directions and mostly disappears from view, leaving the longer red and orange wavelengths to reach our eyes. This is why the sky glows red just as the day ends.
options: Why the Sky Turns Red at Sunset
Why the Atmosphere Is So Thick Near the Ground
quests.correctAnswer: Why the Sky Turns Red at Sunset
quests.hint: Look for the sentence that begins with 'This is why.' What is being explained?
quests.explanation: The passage compares midday with sunset and explains the difference. The midday colors and the thick air are parts of the explanation, not the thing being explained.
quests.whyThisTitle: It names the effect that the light's longer journey through the atmosphere produces.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Before buying a used car, ask to see its service records, which show how well it has been looked after. Drive it on both a highway and a bumpy road to listen for strange noises. If you can, have an independent mechanic inspect it, even if the seller offers a warranty. A low price is tempting, but repair costs can erase the savings quickly.
options: Understanding Car Warranties and Seller Promises
Checking a Used Car Before You Buy
quests.correctAnswer: Checking a Used Car Before You Buy
quests.hint: Ask what the reader is supposed to do with these tips, and when.
quests.explanation: Records, test drives, and inspections are all checks made before a purchase. Warranties are mentioned only in passing, and finding cars is never discussed.
quests.whyThisTitle: The service records, test drive, and inspection are all checks done before the purchase.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Buying clothes second-hand costs far less than buying new, and it keeps usable garments out of the trash. Shoppers also find styles that are no longer in stores. On the downside, sizes are unpredictable, and hunting through crowded racks takes time. Some buyers also worry about wear that is not visible until the item is washed.
options: Finding Unusual Styles at Low Prices
Washing New Clothes Before Wearing Them
The Upsides and Downsides of Second-Hand Clothes
quests.correctAnswer: The Upsides and Downsides of Second-Hand Clothes
quests.hint: Look at the phrase 'on the downside.' How does it shape the passage?
quests.explanation: Low prices and unusual styles are among the benefits, and washing appears among the drawbacks. The passage is built around both sides.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title reflects the two-part structure of benefits followed by drawbacks.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The software team at Delta Works complained that their days were sliced into pieces by meetings, leaving little time to write code. Managers tried shorter meetings, but the interruptions remained. Then they declared Wednesdays meeting-free. Developers report finishing more work, and urgent questions are simply answered in writing.
options: Meeting-Free Wednesdays Give a Team Time to Work
quests.correctAnswer: Meeting-Free Wednesdays Give a Team Time to Work
quests.hint: One solution failed and another worked. Which title reflects the one that worked?
quests.explanation: Shorter meetings were tried and did not solve the problem. The title should name the change that did, together with what it gave the team.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title connects the meeting-free day to the team's regained working time.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Bread dough rises because of yeast, a tiny living organism. When mixed with flour and water, the yeast feeds on sugars and releases gas that gets trapped in the stretchy dough. The dough swells, and after an hour or two it is shaped and baked. The heat of the oven makes the gas expand one last time, then sets the loaf's structure.
options: How Yeast Makes Bread Dough Rise
Baking Bread in a Hot Oven at High Heat
quests.correctAnswer: How Yeast Makes Bread Dough Rise
quests.hint: Ask what makes the dough swell, and what the passage says about it at each stage.
quests.explanation: Baking and shaping are stages that come after the dough has risen. The passage centers on the role of yeast in making it rise.
quests.whyThisTitle: The feeding, the trapped gas, and the final expansion all explain how the dough rises.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Small shops often prefer cash because card companies charge them a fee on every sale. Customers, on the other hand, like cards for convenience and for the record they keep of spending. Some shops now offer a small discount for cash to keep both sides happy. Which method wins often depends on the size of the purchase: cards for large amounts, coins for a cup of coffee.
options: Why Card Fees Hurt Small Shops with Thin Profits
quests.correctAnswer: Cash Versus Cards in Shops
quests.hint: Whose point of view is given, and how many are there?
quests.explanation: Card fees, spending records, and discounts each belong to one side or one solution. The passage sets shop preferences against customer preferences.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice presents the contrast between what shops and customers prefer.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A home emergency kit does not need to be expensive. Start with water, about four liters per person per day, and food that needs no cooking. Add a flashlight, spare batteries, a first-aid kit, and copies of important documents in a waterproof bag. Store everything in one place that all family members know, and check it twice a year to replace expired items.
options: Checking Expiry Dates on Food Supplies Twice a Year
Putting Together a Home Emergency Kit
quests.correctAnswer: Putting Together a Home Emergency Kit
quests.hint: Count the different items and actions. What single job are they part of?
quests.explanation: Water, documents, and expiry checks are all pieces. The passage walks the reader through assembling and keeping the entire kit.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title covers the contents, the storage, and the upkeep as one project.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The beach at Pelham Bay was shrinking every winter as storms carried sand out to sea. Officials planted a long strip of tall grass along the dunes, whose roots hold the sand together, and closed some footpaths to let the plants grow. After three years, the dunes had grown taller, and the beach was no longer losing ground.
options: Using Grass to Protect a Shrinking Beach
Why Beaches Lose Sand Each Winter
quests.correctAnswer: Using Grass to Protect a Shrinking Beach
quests.hint: Separate the problem, the action, and the result.
quests.explanation: Footpath closures support the planting, and storm damage describes only the problem. The passage joins the problem with the grass solution.
quests.whyThisTitle: It links the planted grass to the beach that stopped shrinking.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Online courses let people study at any hour and from any place, which suits workers with unpredictable schedules. They are often cheaper than classes on campus, and recordings can be replayed. But without a teacher in the room, many learners lose motivation halfway. Completion rates for free courses are low, and students who succeed tend to be those who set a routine.
options: Benefits and Drawbacks of Online Courses
Why Campus Classes Cost More Money
Replaying Recorded Lessons Whenever You Like
quests.correctAnswer: Benefits and Drawbacks of Online Courses
quests.hint: Ask which title includes what is good and what is difficult.
quests.explanation: Replays and routines are each one detail, and campus costs are a passing comparison. The passage's structure is a set of advantages followed by a serious drawback.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title matches the passage's two sides: flexible, affordable study and the struggle to stay motivated.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Recycled glass jars are sorted by color at a plant, since mixing colors would give the new glass a muddy shade. Machines then crush them into small pieces called cullet, and magnets and air jets remove metal lids and paper labels. The cullet is melted in a furnace at high temperature and poured into molds to form new bottles. The process can be repeated almost endlessly.
options: How Old Glass Becomes New Bottles
Turning Sand into Glass in a Furnace
Why Glass Is Sorted by Color
quests.correctAnswer: How Old Glass Becomes New Bottles
quests.hint: Trace the glass from the first step to the last.
quests.explanation: Sorting and removing lids are stages, and making glass from sand is never described. The passage follows the recycled glass from jar to new bottle.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title names the full transformation from used jars to new bottles.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Potholes appear when water seeps into small cracks in the road and freezes overnight. Ice takes up more space than water, so it pushes the cracks wider. When the ice melts, it leaves a gap under the surface. Traffic then breaks the weakened patch, and the hole grows. This is why potholes are most common after winter.
options: Why Roads Are Made of Asphalt
quests.correctAnswer: How Frost Makes Potholes
quests.hint: Which title describes the chain of events that the passage lays out?
quests.explanation: Repair and safe driving are responses the passage does not discuss. Each sentence adds another link between freezing and the hole.
quests.whyThisTitle: The freezing, the expanding ice, and the traffic all form one chain that ends in a pothole.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In villages far from a city, a car is often the only way to reach a doctor or supermarket, since buses may come only twice a day. Cars offer freedom but cost a great deal to buy, insure, and fuel. Shared minibuses, run by community groups in some regions, cost less and bring neighbors together, but they follow fixed times and routes. Residents therefore weigh independence against expense.
options: Cars or Minibuses in the Countryside
Visiting the Doctor from a Village
Why Rural Bus Services Are So Rare
The Rising Cost of Fuel for Villagers
quests.correctAnswer: Cars or Minibuses in the Countryside
quests.hint: What two choices does the last sentence sum up?
quests.explanation: Rare buses and fuel costs are single points connected to the choices. The final sentence shows the passage is weighing two ways of getting around.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice presents the two options and the trade-off between freedom and cost.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Act quickly when a stain appears, since fresh marks come out more easily. Blot, do not rub, because rubbing pushes the liquid deeper into the fibers. Rinse from the back of the fabric with cold water, and only use warm water once you know the stain is not protein-based, like blood, which can set with heat. Check the label before using any cleaner.
options: A Guide to Choosing the Best Cleaning Product
First Steps for Removing Fabric Stains
Why Blood Stains Are Especially Hard to Remove
quests.correctAnswer: First Steps for Removing Fabric Stains
quests.hint: Look at how each sentence gives a direction. What is the reader trying to do?
quests.explanation: Cold water and blood are details within the advice. Choosing a cleaner is barely mentioned, only in the last line.
quests.whyThisTitle: All the instructions serve the goal of getting a stain out of fabric, starting with the earliest steps.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Night shifts often pay more, and roads and offices are quieter. Workers may also see their families during the afternoon. But sleeping in daylight is difficult, meals are harder to organize, and social events tend to happen when workers are on duty. Many find the extra pay is worth it for a few years but not for a lifetime.
options: Why Roads Are Quieter at Night
quests.correctAnswer: Working the Night Shift
quests.hint: Ask whether the passage argues for the night shift, against it, or for a balance.
quests.explanation: Sleep, quiet roads, and pay are each part of a larger picture. The passage lists rewards and costs and ends by weighing them.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title covers the pay, the quiet, and the costs to sleep and social life in one topic.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Ms. Okoye noticed that the same three students answered every question while the others stayed quiet. Instead of calling on people at random, she started asking students to talk with a partner for a minute before anyone answered. Suddenly, almost everyone had something to say, and more hands went up.
options: Working with a Partner for a Minute
quests.correctAnswer: Getting Everyone Talking
quests.hint: What was wrong at the start, and how did the teacher change it?
quests.explanation: Working with a partner is the method, but the passage is about the result it produced. The random calling is the approach she abandoned.
quests.whyThisTitle: It captures the shift from three voices to the whole class taking part.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Steel and concrete expand when heated and shrink when cooled. On a long bridge, the change can amount to several centimeters between winter and summer. Without any room to move, the bridge would push against itself and crack. Engineers therefore leave small gaps, filled with flexible material, between sections of the road.
options: Building Bridges with Steel and Concrete
How Engineers Fill Gaps with Flexible Material
Gaps That Let Bridges Handle the Weather
quests.correctAnswer: Gaps That Let Bridges Handle the Weather
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence gives the solution. What question does it answer?
quests.explanation: The flexible filling and the building materials are details. The passage explains why the gaps exist and what would go wrong without them.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title ties the gaps to the expansion and shrinking that make them necessary.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Traveling cheaply is mostly a matter of choosing when and where. Flights and rooms cost less outside school holidays, and a place near the edge of a city can be half the price of one in the center. Eating where locals eat, and walking or using public transport, reduces daily costs further. Booking the most expensive parts, transport and lodging, first tells you how much is left for everything else.
options: Choosing Lodging at the City's Edge
Planning a Trip on a Tight Budget
quests.correctAnswer: Planning a Trip on a Tight Budget
quests.hint: How many separate tips are in the passage, and what do they all aim at?
quests.explanation: Each of the other titles names a single tip. The advice about timing, location, food, and order of booking all aims at lowering total cost.
quests.whyThisTitle: The tips about dates, location, meals, and booking order all serve a low-cost trip.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Students who take handwritten notes tend to summarize as they go, since writing is slower than listening. This effort helps them understand. Typists can capture almost every word, but they sometimes copy without thinking. On the other hand, typed notes are easy to search and share. Some students handwrite in class and type up a cleaned version later, gaining the benefits of both.
options: Taking Notes by Pen or by Keyboard
Copying Word for Word in Class
quests.correctAnswer: Taking Notes by Pen or by Keyboard
quests.hint: Notice how the passage ends. What does it suggest about the two methods?
quests.explanation: Searching, summarizing, and copying are single features. The passage compares handwriting and typing and finishes by combining them.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title represents the comparison, including the last-sentence idea of using both.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Farmers often discard carrots that are crooked and apples that are too small, not because they taste worse but because shops reject them for looks. Some supermarkets now sell these 'imperfect' items at a lower price. Shoppers save money, farmers earn from produce that once went to waste, and less food ends up in landfill.
options: The Cost of Buying Fresh Vegetables
quests.correctAnswer: Selling Odd-Shaped Produce
quests.hint: The passage describes a problem, then a change. Which title contains the change?
quests.explanation: Rejection for looks is the problem, and harvest struggles are not mentioned. The center of the passage is the new practice and its benefits.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice names the practice that reduces waste and helps shoppers and farmers.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Strong essays are built in stages. Writers first collect ideas and decide on one main point they want to make. Next they sketch an outline, ordering their evidence from strongest to weakest or in a logical path. Only then do they draft, saving corrections for the end. Reading the finished draft aloud often reveals awkward sentences that silent reading misses.
options: Building an Essay Step by Step
Finding Good Ideas for a Topic
quests.correctAnswer: Building an Essay Step by Step
quests.hint: Which words tell you that the order of actions matters?
quests.explanation: Outlines, ideas, and reading aloud are each a stage. The words first, next, only then, and finished mark the passage as a sequence from start to end.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title covers all stages, from gathering ideas to reading the completed draft.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Smart speakers answer questions, play music, and control lights with only a voice command, which is especially helpful to people with limited mobility. However, they are always listening for a wake word, and some households are uncomfortable with recordings being stored by a company. Owners can review and delete these recordings, but many never do.
options: Convenience and Privacy Concerns of Smart Speakers
Helping People with Limited Mobility Live More Independently
quests.correctAnswer: Convenience and Privacy Concerns of Smart Speakers
quests.hint: What does the word 'however' introduce?
quests.explanation: Lights, recordings, and mobility are single details. The passage begins with usefulness and turns to a concern about privacy.
quests.whyThisTitle: It joins the usefulness of the devices to the privacy worries that follow.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Pigeons crowded the town square and left droppings on statues and benches. The council first put up spikes, but the birds simply moved to nearby roofs. A better result came from a very different step: asking residents and tourists not to feed them. With less food available, the flock shrank by half within a year.
options: Putting Up Spikes on Rooftops and Ledges
How a Town Cut Its Pigeon Numbers
quests.correctAnswer: How a Town Cut Its Pigeon Numbers
quests.hint: Two solutions are mentioned. Which one does the passage present as successful?
quests.explanation: Spikes are the failed attempt, and cleaning is a consequence of the problem. The passage moves from crowding to the step that actually reduced the flock.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title reflects the whole path from a crowded square to a smaller flock.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: City life offers jobs, theaters, and food from every corner of the world, but it also brings noise, crowding, and high rents. Small towns provide space, quiet, and neighbors who know each other's names, yet they may have fewer job options and slower internet. People who move from one to the other often say they miss what they left behind.
options: City Life and Small-Town Life Side by Side
quests.correctAnswer: City Life and Small-Town Life Side by Side
quests.hint: Are both places treated with equal attention?
quests.explanation: Rents, quiet, and moving are single elements. The passage balances the good and bad of two settings and ends with people who feel torn.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title captures the comparison of the two settings and the conclusion that each has something to miss.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When a bee finds flowers, it returns to the hive and dances. The angle of its dance shows other bees which direction to fly, and the length of the dance shows how far. Within minutes, dozens of workers are heading to the same patch. Without this shared signal, each bee would search alone.
options: How Far a Bee Can Fly
Why Bees Return to the Hive
quests.correctAnswer: How Bees Share Directions
quests.hint: What does the dance accomplish?
quests.explanation: Returning to the hive and flight distance are parts of the explanation. The passage's point is that the dance communicates where to find flowers.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice states what the dance does: pass on directions to other bees.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Before entering the sea, check the flags on the beach, which show whether conditions are safe. Swim between the marked areas, where lifeguards can see you, and never swim alone. If you are caught in a strong current, do not fight it; swim sideways until you are free, then return to shore at an angle. Save your energy by floating if you feel tired.
options: Staying Safe When Swimming in the Sea
Understanding Beach Flags and Warning Signs
quests.correctAnswer: Staying Safe When Swimming in the Sea
quests.hint: Think of the reader as someone about to swim. What do all of these instructions protect against?
quests.explanation: Beach flags and currents are only two of the topics. The instructions cover before, during, and if trouble comes, all in service of safety.
quests.whyThisTitle: The advice about flags, marked areas, currents, and tiredness all concerns being safe in the sea.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Patients who do not speak the local language often struggle to explain their symptoms, and mistakes can be serious. One hospital now offers a phone service that connects staff to a trained interpreter within a minute, in more than forty languages. Doctors say consultations are shorter and patients feel calmer, because they can finally describe what is wrong.
quests.correctAnswer: Helping Patients Be Understood
quests.hint: State the problem, the response, and the benefit in your own words before choosing.
quests.explanation: The forty languages and shorter consultations are details of the answer. The passage is about solving a communication barrier for patients.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title connects the language problem to the interpreter service that resolves it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A familiar smell can bring back a memory with surprising force. Scent signals travel to parts of the brain closely tied to emotion and memory before they reach areas that handle language. That is why the smell of a certain soap might remind someone of a childhood home before they can even say why. Memories linked to smell also tend to feel more emotional than those triggered by sight.
options: Why Smells Can Bring Back Strong Memories
Why Language Is Processed in a Separate Brain Area
quests.correctAnswer: Why Smells Can Bring Back Strong Memories
quests.hint: Which title states the effect and hints at its cause?
quests.explanation: The nose and the childhood home are parts of the picture, not the explanation. The passage explains why scent has such a strong link to memory.
quests.whyThisTitle: It captures the effect, and the brain pathway explanation that supports it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: If your library does not own a book, you can ask for an interlibrary loan. A librarian first searches other libraries' catalogs, then sends a request to the nearest one that has a copy. The book travels by delivery van, usually taking about a week, and you receive a message when it arrives. You can keep it for the normal loan period and return it to your own library.
options: Borrowing a Book from Another Library
Waiting About a Week for a Delivery Van
Returning Borrowed Books to Your Own Library
quests.correctAnswer: Borrowing a Book from Another Library
quests.hint: Follow the book from the request to its return.
quests.explanation: Searching, waiting, and returning are steps. The passage takes the whole process from the request to the return.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title covers the request, the journey, and the return as a single process.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Sharing an apartment cuts rent and bills, and there is usually someone around to talk to or borrow a pan from. Yet privacy is limited, and disagreements about cleaning or noise can build up. Housemates who agree early on a few simple rules, such as when guests may stay over, tend to avoid the worst conflicts.
options: Weighing Up Life in a Shared Apartment
quests.correctAnswer: Weighing Up Life in a Shared Apartment
quests.hint: The word 'yet' signals a change in direction. What comes on either side of it?
quests.explanation: Rules, rent, and kitchen items are individual points. The passage weighs benefits against difficulties and ends with a way to handle the difficulties.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title reflects both sides of shared living and how housemates manage the downside.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A tiny mountain school could not find a physics teacher, so its older students had no chance to study the subject. Now a teacher in a distant city teaches the class by video, while an assistant in the room helps with experiments. Students still ask questions in real time, and the school no longer sends its best pupils away for lessons.
options: Video Teaching for a Small School
quests.correctAnswer: Video Teaching for a Small School
quests.hint: What was missing, and how was it supplied?
quests.explanation: Finding a teacher is the goal that could not be met locally, and the experiments are one detail. The passage is about a remote way of teaching the subject.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice names the video teaching that solved the school's shortage.
